13000:
The term "psychosomatic" is made of two Greek words:

  • Psyche = mind
  • Soma = body

So "psychosomatic" simply means: the mind influencing the body. It describes situations where your thoughts, emotions, beliefs, or mental states cause real, measurable, physical changes in your body. This is not imagination. This is not pretending. The body literally changes because of what the mind believes or feels.

With that foundation, a psychosomatic pregnancy is a condition where a person's mind is so powerfully convinced that they are pregnant — that their body actually begins behaving as if they are pregnant — even though there is no baby, no embryo, and no fertilization at all.
The Core Paradox: Real Symptoms, No Real Pregnancy

This is the part that makes people stop and say "Wait, that's possible?"

Yes, it is. And this is what makes psychosomatic pregnancy one of the most fascinating and clinically important phenomena in all of medicine.

The person is not lying. The person is not faking. The person is not acting. Their body is genuinely producing the same physical signs that a truly pregnant person would experience. The symptoms are 100% real. The pregnancy is 100% absent.

This condition is formally known in medical terminology as pseudocyesis (pronounced: soo-doh-sy-EE-sis), from Greek words meaning "false pregnancy." It has also historically been called false pregnancy or phantom pregnancy.
What Symptoms Actually Appear?

This is where things get remarkable. A person with psychosomatic pregnancy can experience most — or even all — of the following:

1. Missed menstrual periods (amenorrhea)
The monthly cycle actually stops. This happens because the brain signals the body to alter the hormonal environment, and the hormones that normally trigger menstruation get disrupted.

2. A visibly swollen or enlarged abdomen
The belly actually grows. The abdomen distends outward, looking like a baby bump. This can happen due to gas accumulation, fat redistribution, or muscle wall changes driven by altered posture and hormonal signals.

3. Breast changes
The breasts enlarge, become tender, and the nipples may darken — exactly as in real pregnancy. In some cases, the breasts even begin producing a milky discharge, because the brain triggers the release of a hormone called prolactin, which is normally only activated during actual pregnancy or breastfeeding.

4. Nausea and vomiting
Classic morning sickness can appear. The stomach reacts as if the hormonal changes of a real pregnancy are occurring, because in a very real sense, they are.

5. Sensations of fetal movement
This is the most astonishing symptom. The person genuinely feels something moving inside them, similar to what pregnant people describe as "the baby kicking." This is caused by involuntary muscle contractions or heightened sensitivity to normal internal sensations (like bowel movement), which the brain interprets and delivers to conscious experience as baby movement.

6. Weight gain
The person gains weight, especially in the abdominal area.

7. Changes in the cervix and uterus
Even internally, the body begins responding — the uterus may slightly soften and the cervix may undergo minor changes similar to early pregnancy.

8. Hormonal shifts (detectable in blood tests)
Blood hormone levels can actually change. Levels of estrogen, progesterone, and prolactin can shift into ranges resembling early pregnancy.
How Does This Happen? The Mind-Body Science Explained Simply

Your brain is the master control system of your entire body. It does not merely think thoughts in isolation — it constantly communicates with your organs, glands, muscles, and immune system through a complex network of nerves, hormones, and chemical signals.

At the center of this control system sits a small but enormously powerful region of the brain called the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus acts like a command center that regulates most of your body's automatic functions: temperature, hunger, sleep, and crucially — the hormonal system, especially reproduction.

Sitting just below the hypothalamus is the pituitary gland, often called the "master gland," because it releases hormones that directly control the ovaries, uterus, breasts, and other reproductive organs.

Now here is the key mechanism:

When a person's mind becomes intensely, deeply, and persistently convinced of a pregnancy — whether due to desperate desire, overwhelming fear, deep grief, or psychological pressure — the emotional and cognitive centers of the brain (particularly areas like the limbic system and prefrontal cortex) send abnormal stress and belief signals down into the hypothalamus.

The hypothalamus, responding to these powerful signals, begins releasing hormones as if pregnancy were real. It tells the pituitary gland to behave accordingly. The pituitary then signals the ovaries, uterus, and breasts to follow suit. The entire hormonal cascade of pregnancy can be triggered — not by an actual fertilized egg, but by the brain's conviction that one exists.

This is the psychosomatic mechanism: a belief so deeply embedded in the nervous system that it overrides biological reality and rewires the body's chemistry.
What Causes Psychosomatic Pregnancy?

There is rarely a single cause. It is almost always a combination of powerful psychological and emotional factors, sometimes mixed with pre-existing hormonal vulnerabilities. Common underlying causes include:

1. Intense desire to be pregnant
People who desperately want a child — especially those who have struggled with infertility for years — are at higher risk. The desire can become so all-consuming that the mind begins unconsciously manufacturing the pregnancy it craves.

2. Grief after pregnancy loss
A person who has experienced a miscarriage, stillbirth, or infant death may develop psychosomatic pregnancy as the mind's way of psychologically processing — or refusing to accept — that loss.

3. Fear of pregnancy
Paradoxically, an intense fear of being pregnant can trigger the same response. The mind hyper-focuses on the possibility, and the body begins reacting to that obsessive focus.

4. Social and cultural pressure
In societies or families where a woman's value is heavily tied to motherhood and fertility, the immense psychological pressure to become pregnant can trigger the condition.

5. Relationship stress
Wanting to preserve a relationship, satisfy a partner's wishes for a child, or avoid social stigma can be contributing factors.

6. Hormonal imbalances
Pre-existing imbalances in estrogen, progesterone, or prolactin can make the body more susceptible to psychosomatic hormonal disruption.

7. Psychological disorders
In some cases, conditions like severe depression, anxiety disorders, or delusional thinking can contribute. However, most cases of pseudocyesis occur in people without a diagnosable psychiatric disorder — they are simply experiencing an extraordinary psychological response to extraordinary emotional pressure.
Who Can Experience This?

While the condition is most commonly documented in people assigned female at birth, it can occur across genders. It has been documented in:

  • Women across all age groups, including post-menopausal women
  • Adolescents
  • Men (known as Couvade syndrome in a related but distinct form, where male partners of pregnant women develop pregnancy-like symptoms)
  • It occurs across all cultures and has been recorded throughout human history in every part of the world
Critical Distinction: This Is NOT Lying or Faking

This point cannot be overstated, because it is the most commonly misunderstood aspect of this condition.

Malingering is the medical term for deliberately faking illness for a personal gain — such as faking symptoms to get attention, sympathy, or to avoid responsibility. Psychosomatic pregnancy is the complete opposite of this.

The person with psychosomatic pregnancy:

  • Genuinely and sincerely believes they are pregnant
  • Is not consciously manufacturing or exaggerating symptoms
  • Is experiencing real, measurable physical changes
  • Is not in control of what their body is doing
  • Is not deceiving anyone deliberately

To accuse such a person of "faking it" is not only medically inaccurate — it is deeply harmful. They are experiencing a real medical and psychological condition that deserves compassionate, professional care.
How Is It Diagnosed?

Diagnosis typically involves the following steps:

1. Pregnancy test
A urine or blood pregnancy test checks for a hormone called hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin), which is only produced when a real embryo implants in the uterus. In pseudocyesis, this test is usually negative, because there is no real embryo producing hCG. However, in rare cases, hormonal disruption can cause slight hCG elevation, which is why a pregnancy test alone is not fully conclusive.

2. Ultrasound
This is the definitive test. An ultrasound scan of the uterus and pelvis will show absolutely no gestational sac, no embryo, and no fetus. The uterus may appear slightly different but there is no pregnancy. This is the clearest, most conclusive evidence.

3. Hormone blood panel
Doctors may measure levels of estrogen, progesterone, prolactin, and other hormones to understand how far the body's hormonal mimicry has gone and to guide treatment.

4. Psychological assessment
A careful, compassionate psychological evaluation is conducted to understand the emotional and mental factors driving the condition.
How Is It Treated?

Effective treatment addresses both the physical symptoms and the psychological roots simultaneously.

For the physical symptoms:
Once the person is shown clear ultrasound evidence that no pregnancy exists (this must be done with extraordinary sensitivity and care), the physical symptoms often begin to resolve on their own. The body's hormonal levels gradually normalize. Periods may return. The abdominal swelling may reduce. The biological changes reverse because the psychosomatic trigger is interrupted.

For the psychological component:

  • Psychotherapy — particularly cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) — helps the person process the underlying emotional pain, fear, grief, or desire that drove the condition
  • Counseling around infertility, pregnancy loss, or relationship issues, depending on the root cause
  • Support groups for those dealing with infertility or pregnancy loss can be profoundly helpful
  • In cases where depression or anxiety is present, appropriate psychiatric treatment may be included

For hormonal irregularities:
If blood tests show significant hormonal disturbance, medication may be used to gently restore hormonal balance.

The most important thing about treatment is this: the patient must never be made to feel foolish, weak, or dishonest. Their condition is a testament to the extraordinary power of the human mind-body connection, and they deserve every bit as much medical respect and care as any other patient.
A Historical Footnote Worth Knowing

Psychosomatic pregnancy is not a modern discovery. It has been recorded for thousands of years.

Hippocrates, the ancient Greek physician often called the father of medicine, documented cases of false pregnancy around 300 BCE.

One of history's most famous cases is that of Queen Mary I of England (known as "Bloody Mary"), who lived in the 1500s. She reportedly experienced at least two episodes of false pregnancy — complete with a swollen belly, cessation of periods, and fetal movement sensations. Her court, her physicians, and she herself were convinced she was pregnant. No child ever arrived. Historians and medical scholars believe these were classic cases of psychosomatic pregnancy, likely driven by the enormous political, personal, and religious pressure she faced to produce an heir.
The Bigger Lesson: The Mind and Body Are Not Separate

Psychosomatic pregnancy is a striking demonstration of something medicine has increasingly come to understand over the past century: the mind and body are not two separate things. They are one deeply interconnected system.

Your emotions, beliefs, fears, and desires are not merely abstract thoughts floating in your head. They are biological events. They release hormones, alter nerve signals, change organ behavior, and reshape your physical reality. Psychosomatic pregnancy is simply one of the most dramatic and visible illustrations of this truth.

Understanding this condition should inspire not skepticism, but awe — at the sheer, almost incomprehensible power of the human mind over the physical world it inhabits.
13001:
When you call something psychotic, you are saying it relates to, involves, or is caused by a condition called psychosis — a serious state of mind in which a person loses touch with reality.

Think of it this way: most of us, even when extremely upset, confused, or mentally unwell, can still tell the difference between what is real and what is not. A person in a psychotic state cannot do this reliably. Their mind has broken from shared reality in a significant way.
What Exactly Is Psychosis? (You Need This to Understand the Adjective)

Psychosis is not a diagnosis by itself — it is a cluster of symptoms that can appear in several mental health conditions. These symptoms are what make something qualify as "psychotic."

The main symptoms are:

1. Hallucinations
The person perceives something that does not actually exist in the outside world. The most common form is hearing voices — voices that may comment on the person's actions, give commands, or argue with each other. The person is fully convinced these voices are real, external sounds. Visual hallucinations (seeing things that aren't there), and less commonly, sensory hallucinations (feeling things crawling on the skin, smelling things) also occur. Crucially, to the person experiencing them, these feel completely real — indistinguishable from actual perception.

2. Delusions
A delusion is a fixed, false belief that the person holds with absolute certainty, even when presented with clear evidence that it is wrong. What makes a belief a delusion is not simply that it is unusual or mistaken — it is that:

  • It is clearly out of touch with reality.
  • The person cannot be reasoned out of it.
  • It has no basis in their cultural or social context.

Common examples of delusions: believing that strangers on the street are secretly agents spying on you, believing that the news anchor on TV is sending you personal coded messages, believing you are a famous historical figure, or believing that your thoughts are being broadcast out loud for others to hear. These are not metaphors or exaggerations — the person genuinely, unshakeably believes these things are true.

3. Disorganized Thinking
The person's thoughts become fragmented, incoherent, or jump from one unrelated idea to another in ways that don't make logical sense. When they speak, it may be difficult or impossible to follow their train of thought. In severe cases, their speech becomes what's called a "word salad" — words strung together without coherent meaning.

4. Disorganized or Unusual Behavior
The person may act in ways that seem bizarre, unpredictable, or inappropriate to the situation — such as laughing at something tragic, dressing in a highly unusual and contextually strange way, or being unable to carry out basic everyday tasks.

5. Negative Symptoms (less obvious but equally important)
These are the loss of normal functions: loss of emotional expressiveness (the face becomes flat and blank), loss of motivation or drive, social withdrawal, and reduced speech. These are called "negative" not because they are bad (though they are) but because they represent something being taken away from the person's normal functioning.
How "Psychotic" Is Used as an Adjective

The word "psychotic" can describe different things depending on what noun it modifies:

A psychotic person / a psychotic patient — someone who is currently experiencing psychosis or has a condition involving psychosis.

A psychotic episode — a defined period of time during which someone experiences psychotic symptoms. An episode has a beginning and end; it does not have to be permanent.

Psychotic symptoms — the specific symptoms described above (hallucinations, delusions, etc.).

Psychotic disorder — a category of mental health conditions in which psychosis is the primary or defining feature.

Psychotic features — when a condition (like depression or bipolar disorder) includes psychotic symptoms as part of its presentation, those symptoms are called "psychotic features." Example: "major depression with psychotic features" means the person has severe depression and also has delusions or hallucinations.

Several mental health conditions are described as psychotic or can involve psychotic features:

  • Schizophrenia — the most well-known psychotic disorder; involves persistent hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking over an extended period.
  • Schizoaffective disorder — a condition combining features of schizophrenia and a mood disorder (depression or bipolar).
  • Brief psychotic disorder — a sudden but short-lived episode of psychotic symptoms, often triggered by extreme stress.
  • Bipolar disorder with psychotic features — during very severe manic or depressive episodes, a person can develop hallucinations or delusions.
  • Major depressive disorder with psychotic features — a severe form of depression where the person also experiences psychotic symptoms, often delusions consistent with depression (e.g., believing they have committed terrible sins or that they are already dead).
  • Substance-induced psychotic disorder — certain drugs (methamphetamine, cocaine, LSD, cannabis in high doses, alcohol withdrawal) can trigger psychosis.
  • Psychosis due to a medical condition — brain tumors, certain infections, autoimmune conditions, or hormonal disorders can cause psychotic symptoms.

This is very important, because the word is widely misunderstood.

Psychotic ≠ violent or dangerous. This is the biggest misconception. Most people experiencing psychosis are frightened and confused — they are far more likely to be victims of harm than perpetrators. While some specific delusions can very rarely lead to dangerous behavior, the vast majority of psychotic individuals pose no threat to others.

Psychotic ≠ psychopathic. These two words sound similar but refer to completely different things. "Psychopathic" (more precisely: someone with psychopathy or antisocial personality disorder) refers to a person who lacks empathy, manipulates others, and behaves ruthlessly — but who has a clear grip on reality. A psychopath knows full well what is real. A psychotic person, by contrast, has lost their grip on reality, often while being a fundamentally non-manipulative individual.

Psychotic ≠ neurotic. "Neurotic" describes someone who experiences excessive anxiety, worry, or emotional distress — but who is fully aware of what is real. A neurotic person's contact with reality is intact. A psychotic person's is not. These are very different states.

Psychotic ≠ "just being extreme or irrational." In everyday casual speech, people sometimes say things like "my boss is psychotic" to mean "my boss is unreasonably demanding." This is informal slang and is medically inaccurate — it does not mean what the word clinically means. When used in a medical or psychological context, "psychotic" always refers to the specific loss of reality contact described above.

If you ever want to determine whether the word "psychotic" applies to something, ask this one question: Has the person lost contact with shared reality?

If a person is wildly emotional, very irrational, extremely anxious, or even mean and cruel — but they still know what is real and what isn't — the word "psychotic" does not apply to them.

If a person is hearing voices that no one else hears, holding unshakeable beliefs that are clearly false, or genuinely cannot tell what is real — then "psychotic" accurately describes their condition or state.

• "After days without sleep, he developed psychotic symptoms, including hearing voices and believing strangers were following him."
  • "The psychiatrist diagnosed her with a brief psychotic episode triggered by the trauma."
  • "Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder that typically emerges in early adulthood."
  • "Her depression had become so severe that it now included psychotic features — she was convinced she was dying of a disease that tests showed she didn't have."
  • "The drug triggered a psychotic reaction in him, causing hallucinations that lasted for hours."

Psychotic describes anything relating to a state of mind in which a person has lost contact with reality — most distinctively through hallucinations (perceiving things that aren't there) and delusions (holding unshakeable false beliefs) — and it applies to people, episodes, symptoms, disorders, and conditions in which this loss of reality contact is the defining feature.
13002: A psychotic (plural: psychotics) is a person who is experiencing psychosis — a severe mental state in which the person has lost touch with reality. That phrase, "lost touch with reality," is the heart of the word, so it's worth unpacking carefully.
What Does "Lost Touch With Reality" Actually Mean?

Everyone shares the same basic reality. We agree that the chair in a room is a chair, that the person beside us is a real person, that if nobody is speaking, we cannot hear a voice. For a psychotic, this shared reality breaks down. Their mind generates experiences and beliefs that feel completely real and true to them — but are not real or true by any objective measure.

This breakdown shows up in two core ways:
1. Hallucinations

A hallucination is a vivid sensory experience of something that does not actually exist.

  • Auditory hallucinations (the most common): Hearing voices — voices that comment on the person's actions, give them commands, argue with each other, or call their name — when no one is actually speaking.
  • Visual hallucinations: Seeing people, animals, objects, or lights that aren't there.
  • Tactile hallucinations: Feeling sensations on or under the skin — such as insects crawling — when nothing is there.
  • Olfactory or gustatory hallucinations: Smelling or tasting things that have no source.

The critical point: these are not imagination or daydreams. To the psychotic, the voice is as real and clear as any voice you have ever heard. They are not "pretending." Their brain is genuinely generating these perceptions.
2. Delusions

A delusion is a fixed, false belief held with absolute certainty, which the person will not give up even when faced with clear evidence against it.

Common types of delusions:

  • Persecutory delusion: The belief that someone (the government, a neighbour, a secret organisation) is watching, following, or plotting to harm them.
  • Grandiose delusion: The belief that they have extraordinary powers, are a divine figure, have been chosen for a special mission, or possess wealth or talent they don't actually have.
  • Referential delusion: The belief that random events in the world (a stranger coughing, a headline in a newspaper, a car passing) are specifically directed at them or contain hidden messages meant for them.
  • Delusions of control: The belief that an outside force is inserting thoughts into their mind, removing their thoughts, or controlling their body and actions.
  • Somatic delusion: The belief that their body is infested, rotting, transformed, or deeply ill in a way that doctors cannot detect.

No amount of reasoning, evidence, or argument will shake a delusion. The person is not being stubborn; in their mind, the belief is simply true, the way you are certain that the floor under your feet is solid.
3. Disorganised Thinking and Speech

Beyond hallucinations and delusions, a psychotic often cannot think in a connected, logical way. Their speech may:

  • Jump rapidly from one unrelated topic to another (loosening of associations).
  • Become so scrambled that it carries no meaning — a jumble of words and sounds (sometimes called "word salad").
  • Trail off mid-sentence.
  • Coin nonsense words they believe have meaning.

This is not confusion from tiredness or distraction. The underlying machinery of thought itself is disrupted.
A Defining Characteristic: Lack of Insight

One of the most important — and tragic — features of psychosis is that the person typically does not know they are unwell. This is called lack of insight (clinically, anosognosia).

A psychotic genuinely believes their experiences are real. They are not performing. They often do not think they need treatment because, from inside their experience, there is nothing wrong with them — the voices are real, the conspirators are real, their special mission is real. This is what separates psychosis from, say, anxiety or depression, where the person usually knows something is wrong.
What Conditions Make Someone "a Psychotic"?

Psychosis is not itself a diagnosis — it is a symptom or a state that can arise from several different conditions:

  • Schizophrenia: The most well-known condition associated with chronic psychosis. It involves persistent hallucinations, delusions, disorganised thinking, and a gradual withdrawal from normal life.
  • Bipolar disorder: During a severe manic or depressive episode, some people develop psychosis.
  • Major depressive disorder with psychotic features: A very severe depression can include hallucinations or delusions (often of guilt, punishment, or illness).
  • Brief psychotic disorder: A sudden, short-lived episode of psychosis — lasting from a day to a month — sometimes triggered by extreme stress.
  • Substance-induced psychosis: Certain drugs (methamphetamine, cocaine, cannabis in vulnerable individuals, LSD, etc.) or withdrawal from alcohol can trigger psychosis.
  • Medical causes: High fever, brain tumours, epilepsy, severe infections, some autoimmune conditions, and certain vitamin deficiencies can produce psychosis.

So when you call someone "a psychotic," you are identifying what their mind is currently doing (or chronically does) — not specifying which illness caused it.
What a Psychotic Is NOT (Common Misconceptions)

1. "Psychotic" does not mean violent.
This is probably the most damaging misconception. The vast majority of psychotics are not dangerous. They are, more often than not, frightened, confused, and vulnerable. Their risk of becoming a victim of violence is actually higher than that of the general population.

2. "Psychotic" does not simply mean "crazy" or "out of control."
Everyday language uses "psychotic" loosely to mean someone acting wild, angry, or bizarre. This is inaccurate and misleading. A person driving recklessly or having a tantrum is not, in any clinical sense, a psychotic.

3. "Psychotic" is not the same as "psychopathic."
A psychopath (more precisely: someone with antisocial personality disorder) is a person with a persistent pattern of manipulativeness, lack of empathy, and disregard for others. They are very much in touch with reality — in fact, they often exploit it. Psychosis and psychopathy are entirely different phenomena that happen to share a prefix.
Psychotic vs. Neurotic (a Useful Contrast)

These two words are often confused. Here is the clean distinction:

  • A neurotic is someone who is anxious, obsessive, or emotionally troubled, but who remains fully in touch with reality. They know what is real. Their suffering comes from fears and thoughts they cannot control, but they do not hallucinate or hold delusions.
  • A psychotic has lost contact with reality itself. Their suffering comes from a world that is genuinely different — in their perception — from the world everyone else inhabits.

A neurotic fears something that might happen. A psychotic believes something is happening that isn't.
Is Psychosis Treatable?

Yes. Antipsychotic medications can significantly reduce or eliminate hallucinations and delusions. Many people who have experienced psychosis recover well, especially with early treatment. This is why recognising the signs and seeking help quickly matters enormously.
How the Word Is Used

In clinical and medical writing, "a psychotic" is a legitimate term for a person in a psychotic state. However, in modern mental health practice, professionals increasingly prefer person-first language — "a person with psychosis" or "a person experiencing psychosis" — to avoid reducing someone's identity to their diagnosis. Both forms appear in literature; the noun "psychotic" is not wrong, but the person-first phrasing is considered more respectful and humanising.
In Summary

A psychotic is a person whose mind has lost its grip on shared reality — generating experiences (hallucinations) and unshakeable false beliefs (delusions) that feel completely real to them, often without the person realising anything is wrong. It is a state that can arise from several conditions, is not synonymous with violence or dangerousness, is distinct from both neurosis and psychopathy, and is — critically — treatable.
13003:
To understand what a psychotic disorder is, you first need to understand one word: psychosis.

Psychosis is a state in which a person loses touch with reality. This doesn't mean they are unintelligent, weak, or making things up. It means their brain is producing experiences — perceptions, beliefs, thoughts — that do not match the reality that other people around them share. The person experiencing psychosis genuinely cannot tell the difference between what is real and what isn't. To them, their experiences feel completely real.

A psychotic disorder is a category of mental illness in which psychosis is the central, defining feature. These are serious disorders of the brain and mind that significantly disrupt a person's ability to think clearly, feel emotions appropriately, relate to others, and function in daily life.
The Core Symptoms of Psychosis

Psychosis has several recognizable symptoms. These are the building blocks of all psychotic disorders. Medical professionals divide them into two broad groups: positive symptoms and negative symptoms. These labels don't mean "good" and "bad." Instead, positive symptoms refer to things that are added to a person's experience that shouldn't be there, and negative symptoms refer to things that are taken away or diminished from a person's normal functioning.

Positive Symptoms

Hallucinations are experiences of sensing something that doesn't exist in the external world. The most common type is auditory hallucinations — hearing voices. These voices may comment on what the person is doing, give them commands, or have conversations with each other. The person hears these voices just as clearly as they would hear a real person speaking. Visual hallucinations (seeing things that aren't there), olfactory hallucinations (smelling things), tactile hallucinations (feeling sensations on the skin), and gustatory hallucinations (tasting things) also occur but are less common.

Delusions are fixed, false beliefs that a person holds with absolute certainty, despite clear evidence to the contrary, and despite the fact that the belief is not shared by their culture or community. For example, a person might believe that the government has implanted a chip in their brain to monitor their thoughts (a persecutory delusion), or that a news anchor on television is sending them secret personal messages (a referential delusion), or that they are a famous historical figure or have a divine mission (a grandiose delusion), or that their body is rotting from the inside even though they are physically healthy (a somatic delusion). No amount of logical argument will convince the person that their belief is false, because the delusion feels as real to them as any firmly held truth.

Disorganized thinking refers to a breakdown in the logical, ordered way thoughts connect to one another. When a person has disorganized thinking, their speech reveals it. They might jump from one topic to a completely unrelated one mid-sentence (called derailment or loose associations). They might give answers that are vaguely related but never actually address the question (called tangentiality). In severe cases, speech becomes a meaningless jumble of words with no logical connection (called word salad). The person is not choosing to speak this way; their actual thought process has become disorganized.

Disorganized or abnormal behavior means that the person's actions no longer follow a goal-directed, socially appropriate pattern. This might look like childlike silliness in an adult, unpredictable agitation, difficulty completing everyday tasks like cooking or dressing, or behaving in bizarre ways that make no sense to observers.

Catatonia is a particular type of abnormal behavior that deserves its own mention. In catatonia, a person may become physically rigid and unresponsive to the environment, hold unusual postures for long periods, become mute, or at the other extreme, engage in excessive, purposeless movement. It reflects a profound disruption in the brain's control over voluntary movement and responsiveness.

Negative Symptoms

Flat affect (or blunted affect) means a dramatic reduction in the outward expression of emotion. The person's face becomes expressionless, their voice becomes monotone and robotic, and they show little reaction even to things that would normally make someone smile, laugh, or cry. This is not because they don't feel emotions inside — it's because the brain's ability to express those emotions outwardly is impaired.

Alogia is a severe reduction in the amount of speech. The person gives very brief, empty replies. This isn't shyness; the brain's capacity to generate language and thought is diminished.

Avolition is a loss of motivation and the inability to initiate or sustain goal-directed activities. The person may sit for hours without doing anything, neglect personal hygiene, stop pursuing hobbies, or stop going to work or school. Again, this is not laziness — it reflects a brain that has lost the drive circuitry needed to motivate action.

Anhedonia is the inability to experience pleasure. Things that the person used to enjoy — music, food, socializing, sex — no longer feel rewarding or enjoyable.

Social withdrawal is a marked decrease in interest in and engagement with other people, which worsens isolation.

Negative symptoms are often harder for outsiders to recognize and are sometimes mistaken for depression or laziness. They are, however, core features of many psychotic disorders and are often more resistant to treatment than positive symptoms.
Why Does Psychosis Happen in the Brain?

Psychosis arises from disruptions in how the brain processes and interprets information. While the full picture is still being studied, the science points to several contributing factors:

Neurotransmitter dysregulation is central. Dopamine, a chemical messenger in the brain involved in reward, motivation, and salience (meaning the sense of how important or significant something is), becomes dysregulated. In psychosis, the dopamine system is often overactive in certain pathways, causing the brain to assign enormous significance and meaning to random, irrelevant stimuli — which is thought to contribute to the formation of delusions. Glutamate, another neurotransmitter, is also implicated. Serotonin plays a role as well, particularly in the cases where mood and psychosis overlap.

Brain structure and connectivity are also involved. Studies using brain imaging show that people with certain psychotic disorders have subtle abnormalities in the structure of their brains — changes in the volume of certain regions, altered connectivity between regions, and differences in white matter (the brain's internal "wiring"). The prefrontal cortex, which governs planning, judgment, and logical reasoning, often shows reduced activity in people experiencing psychosis.

Genetics plays a significant role. Having a close biological relative with a psychotic disorder substantially increases one's risk. However, no single gene causes psychosis — it involves many genes, each contributing a small amount of risk. Genetics loads the gun; environment pulls the trigger.

Environmental and life factors can trigger psychosis in those who are biologically predisposed. These include severe stress, trauma (especially in childhood), being born in winter (possibly related to prenatal infections), urban upbringing, immigration, cannabis use (particularly heavy, early use of high-potency cannabis), and other drug use. Obstetric complications during birth have also been implicated.

Medical conditions can directly cause psychosis by affecting the brain. These include epilepsy, autoimmune encephalitis (where the immune system attacks the brain), brain tumors, severe infections like meningitis or encephalitis, thyroid disorders, vitamin B12 deficiency, Huntington's disease, and many others.
The Different Types of Psychotic Disorders

"Psychotic disorder" is not a single diagnosis — it's an umbrella term for a family of related disorders. Here are the main ones:

Schizophrenia

Schizophrenia is the best-known and most extensively studied psychotic disorder. It is a chronic, severe mental illness that typically emerges in late adolescence or early adulthood — slightly earlier in males (late teens to mid-20s) than in females (mid-20s to early 30s). It affects roughly 1% of the global population across all cultures.

For a diagnosis of schizophrenia, a person must have experienced significant symptoms — including at least one of the following three: delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech — for at least six months, and these symptoms must significantly impair their functioning at work, in relationships, or in self-care. Negative symptoms are also prominent and are, in many cases, more disabling than the positive symptoms.

Schizophrenia is a lifelong condition, but it does not follow a single predictable course. Some people experience a few episodes and then do well with treatment. Others have persistent symptoms. Many improve significantly over time. The old belief that schizophrenia inevitably leads to permanent deterioration has been shown to be incorrect.

Schizoaffective Disorder

This is a disorder in which a person experiences both psychotic symptoms (like those in schizophrenia) and significant mood episodes — either depression or mania (or both). The key distinction from other conditions is that the psychotic symptoms must occur for a substantial period of time independently of the mood episodes, meaning the psychosis isn't only present during a depressive or manic phase. Schizoaffective disorder sits conceptually between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder with psychotic features.

Schizophreniform Disorder

This is essentially a shorter-duration version of schizophrenia. The symptoms are the same, but they have lasted between one month and six months. If the symptoms persist beyond six months, the diagnosis is changed to schizophrenia. Some people fully recover after one episode; for others, it becomes schizophrenia.

Brief Psychotic Disorder

This involves the sudden onset of one or more psychotic symptoms — delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or disorganized behavior — that last at least one day but less than one month, after which the person returns to their normal level of functioning. It is often triggered by severe stress (like a traumatic event or the death of a loved one), and it is not attributable to a medical condition or substance use.

Delusional Disorder

In delusional disorder, the person has one or more persistent delusions, but the rest of their thinking and behavior remains largely intact. Unlike schizophrenia, they do not have prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech, or significant negative symptoms. They can often function quite well in everyday life — holding jobs, maintaining relationships — while simultaneously holding a fixed false belief that is completely disconnected from reality. Common types of delusional disorder include the belief that one is being followed or poisoned (persecutory), the belief that a celebrity is secretly in love with them (erotomanic), the belief that one's partner is cheating (jealous), and the belief that one has a serious physical illness (somatic).

Substance or Medication-Induced Psychotic Disorder

Psychosis that is directly caused by the use of substances — including alcohol withdrawal, amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis (especially in high doses or with repeated use), LSD, PCP, and others — or by medications (such as corticosteroids, some anticonvulsants, or certain other drugs). The psychosis resolves once the substance is cleared from the body or the offending medication is stopped, though in some cases it can persist.

Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

Psychosis that is the direct physiological result of a medical condition — such as a brain tumor, epilepsy, autoimmune encephalitis, thyroid disease, lupus affecting the brain, or metabolic disturbances. Treating the underlying condition is the primary approach, though anti-psychotic medication may also be used in the meantime.
What Psychotic Disorders Are Not

This is important, because the word "psychotic" is widely misused in everyday language.

A psychotic disorder is not the same as a personality disorder. For instance, antisocial personality disorder (sometimes colloquially and incorrectly called "psychopathic") has nothing to do with psychosis.

Psychosis is not the same as being "crazy" in the casual, pejorative sense. People with psychotic disorders are not fundamentally different or less human. Their brains are experiencing a medical disruption.

People with psychotic disorders are not inherently dangerous. The popular cultural image of the violent, dangerous "psychotic" is not supported by evidence when properly studied. The overwhelming majority of people with psychotic disorders are not violent, and they are far more likely to be the victims of violence than the perpetrators. When violence does occur in connection with psychosis, it is often associated with untreated illness, substance use, or specific circumstances rather than psychosis itself.

Psychosis is not the same as dissociation. Dissociation involves feeling detached from one's thoughts, feelings, surroundings, or sense of identity — a disconnect from one's own experience. Psychosis involves mistaken beliefs about and perceptions of external reality.

Psychotic disorder is not the same as intellectual disability. Intelligence is not impaired as a core feature of psychotic disorders, though cognitive difficulties in attention, memory, and processing speed are common secondary effects.
How Psychotic Disorders Are Diagnosed

There is no blood test, brain scan, or genetic test that definitively diagnoses a psychotic disorder. Diagnosis is made by a trained mental health professional — usually a psychiatrist — through:

A detailed clinical interview, where the professional asks about the person's symptoms, their onset and duration, their family history, any substance use, and their overall level of functioning.

Mental status examination, which assesses appearance, behavior, speech, mood, thought process, thought content (delusions), perceptual disturbances (hallucinations), cognition, and insight.

Medical investigations to rule out physical causes — including blood tests (thyroid function, vitamin levels, metabolic panel, drug screen), and sometimes an MRI or EEG, depending on what the clinical picture suggests.

Diagnosis uses criteria from classification systems, most commonly the DSM-5-TR (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association) or the ICD-11 (International Classification of Diseases, published by the World Health Organization).

A key concept in diagnosis is duration and impairment. How long have the symptoms been present? Have they disrupted the person's ability to function? The answers to these questions distinguish between, say, brief psychotic disorder and schizophrenia.

Another key concept is exclusion. Before a primary psychotic disorder is diagnosed, the clinician must rule out that the psychosis is caused by a substance, a medication, or a medical condition.
How Psychotic Disorders Are Treated

Psychotic disorders are treatable. Many people achieve remission of their symptoms and lead meaningful, fulfilling lives. Treatment typically involves a combination of the following:

Antipsychotic Medication

These are the cornerstone of treatment. They work primarily by modulating dopamine activity in the brain. There are two generations:

First-generation (typical) antipsychotics, developed in the 1950s, include drugs like haloperidol and chlorpromazine. They are effective for positive symptoms but carry a significant risk of side effects involving movement — tremors, rigidity, restlessness, and a serious long-term risk called tardive dyskinesia (involuntary, repetitive movements).

Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics, developed from the 1990s onward, include drugs like olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, aripiprazole, and clozapine. They generally have a lower risk of movement-related side effects, but many carry risks of metabolic side effects — weight gain, elevated blood sugar, and increased risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic, reserved for cases that don't respond to other medications, but requires regular blood monitoring because of a rare but serious risk of reducing white blood cells.

Finding the right medication often involves some trial and error, as response to antipsychotics varies between individuals.

Psychotherapy

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Psychosis (CBTp) is a form of therapy specifically adapted for psychotic disorders. It helps people examine the evidence for their delusional beliefs, develop coping strategies for hallucinations, challenge unhelpful thought patterns, and reduce distress. It does not aim to "argue away" delusions but rather to help the person develop a more flexible relationship with their experiences.

Family therapy and psychoeducation are critically important. When family members understand the illness — its nature, its treatment, and how to respond helpfully — outcomes for the person with the disorder improve significantly. High "expressed emotion" in families (criticism, hostility, over-involvement) is a known predictor of relapse; helping families reduce this improves outcomes.

Social skills training helps people rebuild the interpersonal skills that may have been eroded by the illness.

Supported employment programs help people with psychotic disorders return to or maintain work, which is associated with better outcomes.

Hospitalization

During an acute psychotic episode, especially when the person poses a risk to themselves or others, or is unable to care for themselves, inpatient hospitalization may be necessary to stabilize the person safely, begin or adjust medication, and ensure they receive intensive monitoring and support.

Community and Social Support

Long-term recovery is not just about medication. Stable housing, meaningful daily activities, supportive relationships, and social integration are all associated with better outcomes. Many countries have community mental health teams, assertive community treatment (ACT) programs, and peer support workers (people with lived experience of psychosis who support others) that play an important role.
What Affects Prognosis?

Prognosis — the expected course and outcome of the disorder — varies widely and is shaped by many factors:

Earlier treatment leads to better outcomes. The period between the first appearance of psychotic symptoms and when treatment begins is called the Duration of Untreated Psychosis (DUP). Research consistently shows that a shorter DUP is associated with faster recovery, better response to treatment, and better long-term functioning. This is why early intervention programs for psychosis are considered a major public health priority.

Acute onset (symptoms that develop suddenly) tends to have a better prognosis than insidious onset (symptoms that creep in slowly over time).

Good premorbid functioning — having had good social, academic, and occupational functioning before the illness began — is associated with a better outcome.

Prominent negative symptoms tend to be associated with a less favorable course.

Insight — the person's awareness that they are unwell and need treatment — is crucial. Poor insight is one of the biggest barriers to treatment adherence. It is not stubbornness; impaired insight is itself a symptom of the disorder.

Substance use worsens outcomes significantly. Cannabis use in particular is strongly associated with triggering psychosis, worsening symptoms, increasing the frequency of relapse, and reducing response to treatment.

Social support is a powerful protective factor. People with strong relationships and stable social environments do better than those who are isolated.
Insight: A Concept Worth Understanding Deeply

One of the most philosophically interesting and clinically important features of psychotic disorders is the concept of insight — the person's own awareness that their experiences (the voices, the beliefs, the perceptions) are products of a mental illness rather than real events.

Insight exists on a spectrum. Some people with psychotic disorders have full insight: they know the voice they hear isn't real, they know their belief that they're being followed is a symptom, and they actively cooperate with treatment. Others have partial insight: they might acknowledge they were ill in hindsight but can't recognize it during an active episode. Others have minimal or absent insight: they are utterly convinced that their experiences are real and that those trying to help them are wrong or even conspiring against them.

This matters enormously because it drives treatment adherence. Someone who doesn't believe they are ill will see no reason to take medication or attend therapy. This is called anosognosia when it's particularly severe and unyielding — it's not denial in the psychological sense, but rather a symptom of the brain illness itself, where the brain's self-monitoring systems are impaired.
A Note on Stigma

Psychotic disorders carry a heavy burden of stigma — in popular media, in everyday language, and even within healthcare settings. Words like "psycho," "schizo," and "lunatic" are used as insults, deeply misrepresenting what these illnesses actually are and causing real harm to people who live with them.

The truth is that psychotic disorders are brain-based medical conditions with known neurobiological substrates, identifiable risk factors, evidence-based treatments, and variable but often meaningful prospects for recovery. People with psychotic disorders are not defined by their illness. They have identities, relationships, dreams, and the capacity for a meaningful life. Stigma delays help-seeking, worsens outcomes, and causes unnecessary suffering.
Summary: The Essence of the Term

A psychotic disorder is a medical condition of the brain in which a person loses touch with shared reality, experiencing symptoms such as hallucinations (perceiving things that aren't there), delusions (holding false, unshakeable beliefs), disorganized thinking, abnormal behavior, and negative symptoms like loss of motivation and emotional expression. These disorders exist in several forms — including schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, brief psychotic disorder, delusional disorder, and others — each differentiated by the nature, severity, combination, and duration of symptoms, as well as their underlying cause. They arise from a complex interplay of genetic vulnerability, brain neurochemistry, developmental factors, and environmental triggers. They are serious, but they are treatable, and many people with these conditions live meaningful, productive lives.
13004: A pterodactyl is a type of flying reptile that lived millions of years ago and is now completely extinct. Think of it like a giant lizard with wings — something like a dragon, but real.

What exactly is it?

A pterodactyl is a prehistoric flying reptile that soared through the skies during the age of dinosaurs. It had large wings, a long beak (often filled with teeth), and clawed limbs. It was a real, living creature — not a myth — and fossils of it have been found all over the world.

The wings were not made of feathers like a bird's wings. Instead, they were made of a thin, leathery skin membrane — like a bat's wings — stretched across an extremely long finger bone and attached to the body. This membrane was tough but lightweight, allowing the animal to fly.

Was it a dinosaur?

This is one of the most common misunderstandings about this word, and it is important to get it right.

No. A pterodactyl was not a dinosaur. It lived alongside dinosaurs during the same era, but it belonged to a completely separate group of animals called pterosaurs (flying reptiles). Dinosaurs, by scientific definition, were land animals. Pterodactyls ruled the skies while dinosaurs ruled the land, and different creatures ruled the seas.

Everyday use vs. Scientific use

The word "pterodactyl" is actually used in two slightly different ways, and knowing both will help you understand it completely:

1. In everyday/casual language, people use "pterodactyl" loosely to mean any large, flying prehistoric reptile. When someone in a movie, a book, or a cartoon says "pterodactyl," they usually just mean one of those big, winged, ancient flying creatures in general.

2. In science, "pterodactyl" refers more precisely to a specific genus (a scientific grouping) called Pterodactylus — a relatively small flying reptile, roughly the size of a seagull, that lived about 150 million years ago during the Jurassic period.

Here's where it gets interesting: the large, iconic flying reptile that most people picture when they hear "pterodactyl" — the one with a huge crest on its head and a wingspan as wide as a car — is actually a different animal called a Pteranodon. Pteranodon was much bigger, lived during the Cretaceous period, and had no teeth (unlike the true Pterodactylus). But because people use "pterodactyl" loosely, these two creatures get mixed up all the time.

So when you hear the word in everyday life, it generally just means a big flying reptile from the age of dinosaurs. In a scientific context, it means that one specific, smaller creature.

What were they like?

  • Size: Pterodactyls varied enormously. Some were as small as a sparrow. Others, like the giant Quetzalcoatlus, had wingspans of up to 10–11 meters (roughly 35 feet) — wider than a school bus is long — making them among the largest flying animals that ever existed.
  • Diet: Many pterodactyls ate fish, scooping them from the water with their long beaks. Others ate insects or small animals.
  • Flight: They were likely strong fliers and could soar on air currents, similar to how large birds like eagles and albatrosses fly today.
  • Bone structure: Their bones were hollow and lightweight, much like modern birds, which helped keep them light enough to fly despite sometimes being enormous.
  • Crests: Many species had distinctive bony crests on their heads. Scientists believe these may have been used for attracting mates or regulating body heat.

When did they live, and what happened to them?

Pterodactyls (and all pterosaurs) lived during the Mesozoic Era, which spans three periods:

  • The Triassic (when pterosaurs first appeared, about 228 million years ago)
  • The Jurassic (when they flourished)
  • The Cretaceous (when the most famous large ones, like Pteranodon, lived)

They went extinct approximately 66 million years ago, at the same time as the non-bird dinosaurs, almost certainly due to the catastrophic asteroid impact that dramatically changed Earth's climate and wiped out a massive proportion of life on the planet.

How is the word used in a sentence?

  • "The museum had a complete skeleton of a pterodactyl hanging from the ceiling."
  • "In the film, the explorers were attacked by a flock of pterodactyls swooping down from the cliffs."
  • "Pterodactyls were not dinosaurs, though they lived during the same era."
  • "She let out a scream so loud and sharp that her friends jokingly called it a pterodactyl screech." (a humorous, informal use — high-pitched and prehistoric-sounding!)

The One-Line Summary

A pterodactyl is an extinct, winged reptile — not a dinosaur — that flew through prehistoric skies millions of years ago, with leathery wings, a long beak, and in some species, an enormous size that made it the largest flying creature to ever exist on Earth.
13005:
Pubescent is an adjective that primarily means going through puberty or having recently reached puberty.

To fully understand this word, you first need to understand what puberty is. Puberty is the stage of life — typically between the ages of roughly 8 and 16, though it varies — when a child's body begins physically transforming into an adult body. During this time, the body becomes capable of sexual reproduction. This is a universal biological process that happens to all humans. The word "pubescent" simply describes something or someone that is in that stage, or characteristic of that stage.

Think of it like a spectrum of human development:

  • Child → not yet pubescent
  • Going through the changes of growing up → pubescent
  • Fully grown adult → post-pubescent (or simply adult)

So if you say "a pubescent boy," you mean a boy who is actively going through the physical and hormonal changes of growing up — voice cracking, body hair appearing, growth spurts, and so on.

"Pubescent" is a formal, clinical, or academic word. You would mostly encounter it in:

  • Medical or scientific writing
  • Academic discussions about adolescent development
  • Psychology or biology textbooks

It is not a casual, everyday word. People in everyday speech tend to say "a teenager" or "an adolescent" instead. But "pubescent" is more precise because it specifically points to the biological process of physical maturation, not just an age range.

Example sentences:

  • "The study examined the dietary needs of pubescent children."
  • "Pubescent individuals experience significant hormonal changes."
  • "The clinic specializes in treating pubescent patients."

This is important. "Pubescent" describes a biological stage, not a personality, a behavior, or a social identity. It is a neutral, descriptive word — like saying someone has a fever. It carries no judgment. It simply states a physical reality about where someone is in their biological development.

It also does not mean the same as:

  • "Immature" — immaturity is about behavior or emotional development. Pubescent is about physical/biological development only.
  • "Young" or "childish" — these are vague. Pubescent is specific to the biological window of development.
  • "Adolescent" — adolescence is broader. It refers to the overall social, emotional, and psychological journey of growing up (roughly ages 10–19). Pubescent is narrower — it refers specifically to the physical/biological changes of that period.

"Pubescent" has a second, entirely separate meaning used in biology and botany. In this context, it means covered with fine, soft, short hairs or a downy fuzz. This applies to the surfaces of plants (leaves, stems, fruits), insects, and other organisms.

For example:

  • "The underside of the leaf was pubescent, giving it a velvety texture."
  • "The pubescent stem of the plant helped it retain moisture."

This meaning is used exclusively in scientific descriptions of living things. You would not use it this way in everyday conversation.

Interestingly, both meanings connect at a subtle level — the fine downy hair that appears on the bodies of adolescents during puberty shares the same quality being described in plants. But treat these as two distinct usages depending on your context (human development vs. biology/botany).

ContextWhat "Pubescent" Means
Describing a personGoing through puberty; the physical stage of maturing from child to adult
Describing a plant, leaf, or insectCovered with fine, soft hair or fuzz

The one-line takeaway: Pubescent means relating to or undergoing the biological process of puberty in humans, or — in a scientific context — covered with fine, soft hair. It is a precise, formal word, not a casual one.
13006: "Publication" is all about one central idea: making something available to the public. Everything this word means connects back to that idea. Once you understand that core, the rest falls into place naturally.

The word "publication" is used in two distinct but closely related ways.

Meaning 1 — The Act or Process of Making Something Public

In this sense, "publication" refers to the event, action, or process of officially releasing something so that people can access it. It's not a thing you can hold — it's something that happens.

Think of it this way: imagine you write a book. For months, it exists only on your computer. Nobody can read it. Then, one day, it is printed, distributed to bookstores, and made available to everyone. That moment — or the entire process leading up to it — is called the publication of your book.

Examples:

  • "The publication of her findings changed the field of medicine forever."

Here, "publication" means the act of releasing her research to the world.

  • "The publication of the government report was delayed by several months."

Here, it means the process of making the report officially available to the public.

  • "After publication, the article received thousands of comments."

Here, "after publication" means after it was made public / after it went live.

Key point: In this meaning, you'll often hear phrases like "the publication of [something]" — the publication of a novel, the publication of a study, the publication of new guidelines.

Meaning 2 — A Printed or Digital Item That Has Been Published

In this sense, "publication" refers to an actual item — something you can read, hold, or access — that has been produced and made available to people. This is the "thing" or "object" meaning of the word.

Any book, magazine, newspaper, journal, report, newsletter, or similar work that is produced and distributed to readers is called a publication.

Examples:

  • "This magazine is a well-respected weekly publication."

Here, "publication" simply means the magazine itself — a thing that is published on a regular basis.

  • "She works for a large publishing house that produces over 200 publications a year."

Here, "publications" means all the books, magazines, and other works they produce.

  • "He submitted his research paper to a scientific publication."

Here, "publication" means a scientific journal — a type of periodical where researchers share their work.

Because "publication" simply means something that has been published and made available to the public, it covers a very wide range of items, including:

  • Books — fiction, non-fiction, textbooks, guides
  • Newspapers — daily or weekly news papers
  • Magazines — periodicals covering topics like fashion, science, sports, etc.
  • Academic / Scientific Journals — formal periodicals where researchers publish their studies
  • Reports — official documents produced by governments, companies, or organisations
  • Newsletters — short, regular publications sent to a specific audience
  • Pamphlets and brochures — short printed documents, often for information or advertising
  • Digital publications — online articles, e-books, and digital versions of the above
An Important Use in Academic and Professional Contexts

If someone is a researcher, scientist, or academic, the word "publications" takes on a very specific meaning in their world: it refers to the list of papers, studies, and books they have authored or co-authored. When applying for a job in academia or research, people are asked to list their "publications" — meaning all the works they have officially contributed to the scholarly world.

  • "Professor Sharma has over 50 publications in leading medical journals."

This means he has authored or co-authored over 50 papers/studies that have been formally released in scientific journals.

In formal, legal, or governmental contexts, "publication" can also mean the official announcement or communication of something to the general public. This is still rooted in the same core idea of making something known publicly, but it applies to laws, notices, and formal declarations.

  • "The publication of the new law in the official gazette made it legally binding."

Here, "publication" means the official act of announcing and recording the law so that the public is informed and it becomes enforceable.

It helps to see the two meanings as two sides of the same coin:

  • Meaning 1 is the action → "The publication of the book took two years."
  • Meaning 2 is the result → "The book is now a popular publication."

In both cases, the word is anchored to the same idea: something being made available to the public. Meaning 1 describes the act of doing so. Meaning 2 describes the item that results from doing so.

• "In publication" — something is currently published and available to the public
  • "The journal has been in publication since 1980."
  • "Out of publication" (also "out of print") — something is no longer being produced or made available
  • "That edition went out of publication years ago."
  • "Upon publication" — at the moment it was made public
  • "The book became a bestseller upon publication."
  • "Pending publication" — not yet released, but soon to be
  • "The findings are pending publication in a medical journal."

"Publication" is a noun that means either:

  1. The act of making something available to the public (a process or event), or
  2. A work that has been made available to the public (a book, magazine, journal, report, etc.)

Both meanings share the same root idea: something going from private to public — from unseen to available for all to read, access, or know about.
13007:
Publicity means attention from the public. When people — a large number of them — notice, talk about, or are made aware of someone or something, that is publicity.

Think of it this way: imagine you live in a small town and you do something remarkable — say, you rescue a child from a burning building. The next day, everyone in town is talking about you. The local newspaper runs a story about you. People who have never met you now know your name. That wide, public attention you are receiving? That is publicity.
The Two Sides of the Word

Publicity has two closely connected meanings that often overlap. Understanding both will give you the full picture.

Meaning 1: The attention itself

This is publicity used as an outcome or a state — the condition of being widely known or noticed.

Publicity in this sense is simply the fact that the public is paying attention to something. It doesn't matter why or how — what matters is that a large number of people are aware of it.

Examples:

  • A new movie gets a lot of publicity before its release, because everyone is talking about it and news outlets are covering it.
  • A politician involved in a scandal receives huge amounts of publicity.
  • A small bakery suddenly goes viral on social media and gets unexpected publicity.

Key insight: Publicity can be good or bad. This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. You will often hear phrases like "good publicity" and "bad publicity." When a company launches a wonderful product and the world praises it, that is good publicity. When a celebrity is caught doing something shameful and the media covers it heavily, that is bad publicity. Either way, it is still called publicity — because the word itself is neutral. It simply refers to the amount and nature of public attention, not whether that attention is positive or negative.

There is even a famous saying: "There is no such thing as bad publicity." This means some people believe that even negative attention is better than being ignored entirely, because at least people know your name. (Not everyone agrees with this, but the saying shows just how central the idea of "being noticed" is to the word.)

Meaning 2: The activity of creating that attention

This is publicity used as a process or profession — the deliberate work of making someone or something widely known to the public.

Here, publicity refers to what publicists, marketing teams, and public relations (PR) professionals do. It is the planned effort to spread information about a person, product, company, event, or cause so that the public becomes aware of it.

Examples:

  • A book publisher organizes a publicity campaign for a new novel — sending review copies to journalists, arranging interviews for the author, and getting the book mentioned in magazines.
  • A charity launches a publicity drive to raise awareness about hunger.
  • A startup hires a publicity firm to get their product featured in the news.

Key insight: In this sense, publicity is about strategy and intention. Someone is actively working to attract public attention.
Publicity vs. Advertising — An Important Difference

Many learners confuse publicity with advertising. They are related, but they are not the same thing.

  • Advertising is paid. A company pays a TV channel to run its commercial, or pays a website to display its banner. The company controls exactly what is said, how it looks, and when it appears.
  • Publicity is typically earned, not paid. It comes from journalists writing about you, people sharing your story, or word spreading naturally. You do not directly control what is said about you.

This is why publicity is often considered more powerful and trustworthy than advertising — it comes from an independent voice, not from the person or company themselves.

One subtle but important point: publicity, by its nature, always involves the public — meaning a large, general audience. It is not about one person telling another person something privately. It is about wide, open, large-scale awareness.

This is what separates publicity from, say, a rumour shared between two friends. A rumour becomes publicity only when it spreads far and wide and reaches a large portion of the public.
How the Word Is Used — Common Patterns

Here are the most common ways you will encounter the word "publicity" in real life:

  • "generate publicity" — to create or attract public attention
  • "receive/get publicity" — to be the subject of public attention
  • "seek publicity" — to actively try to be noticed
  • "avoid publicity" — to try to stay out of the public eye
  • "publicity stunt" — a dramatic or unusual act done purely to attract media and public attention (often seen as gimmicky)
  • "publicity campaign" — an organised effort over a period of time to make something widely known
  • "no publicity is bad publicity" — the belief that any attention, even negative, is beneficial

SenseWhat it means
Publicity as a stateThe public attention that a person, product, or event receives
Publicity as an activityThe deliberate effort to make someone or something known to the public

(Note: Both senses are just two ways of looking at the same idea — one is the result, the other is the process of getting there.)

In short: Publicity is both the spotlight (the attention the public gives you) and the work of switching that spotlight on (the effort to make people aware). Whether it happens naturally or is carefully planned, and whether the attention is positive or negative, the wide awareness of the public is what makes it publicity.
13008:
To publicize something means to deliberately spread information about it so that a large number of people become aware of it.

When you publicize something, you are not just quietly mentioning it to a few people. You are actively making an effort to bring it to the attention of the general public — often through media, advertisements, announcements, social platforms, or any other channel that reaches many people at once.

Think of it this way: if you organize a music concert and you want people to come, you don't just sit quietly and hope they find out. You put up posters, post on social media, contact newspapers, and tell everyone you can. That whole effort is publicizing the concert.

A crucial part of understanding "publicize" is that the action is intentional. Someone chooses to publicize something because they want people to know about it. There is always a purpose — it could be to attract an audience, gain support, sell something, raise awareness, or shape people's opinions.

This is what separates "publicize" from simply "telling" someone something. When you publicize, you are making a calculated, deliberate push to widen the circle of people who know about a thing.

Publicizing is always aimed at a broad audience — not one person, not a small group, but the public at large (or at least a large, specific group of people). The word carries a sense of scale. A private whisper is not publicizing. A press release, a campaign, a viral post — those are publicizing.
Connotation — is it positive, negative, or neutral?

The word itself is neutral, but the context gives it its tone.

  • Most often, publicizing is intentional and seen as a positive or neutral effort. A charity publicizes its fundraising drive. An author publicizes their new book. A government body publicizes new safety guidelines.
  • But "publicize" can also carry a negative tone when someone's mistakes, scandals, or private information are spread widely without their desire — or even against it. For example: "The press publicized the politician's financial misconduct." Here, the politician did not want it publicized, but it was. The word itself doesn't judge; it simply describes what happened — the information reached the public.

So: who is doing the publicizing, and what they are publicizing, is what determines whether the connotation feels positive or negative.
How publicize differs from similar words

Understanding nearby words helps sharpen the exact meaning:

Publicize vs. Announce
To announce is to make a single, often formal statement about something — one act, one moment. To publicize is a sustained, repeated effort. You announce a decision at a press conference. You publicize it through weeks of media coverage, interviews, and social posts. Announcing is a moment; publicizing is a campaign.

Publicize vs. Advertise
Advertising is specifically about promoting something for commercial or sales purposes. Publicizing is broader — it can be used for causes, events, ideas, research findings, and products alike. All advertising publicizes, but not all publicizing is advertising.

Publicize vs. Publish
To publish something (a book, an article) is to make it available — to put it out into the world. To publicize it is to actively draw attention to the fact that it exists and to encourage people to engage with it. You can publish a book quietly, with no promotion whatsoever. Publicizing is what you do to make sure people actually notice it.

Publicize vs. Spread
"Spread" is more casual and doesn't imply the same deliberate intent. Rumors spread. News spreads. But these things can happen on their own, without anyone's plan. Publicizing is always a conscious, organized effort.
Where you will commonly see it used

Here are the kinds of contexts where "publicize" most naturally appears:

  • Events and campaigns: "The organization publicized its annual charity run through flyers and social media."
  • Products and releases: "The studio heavily publicized the film months before it released."
  • Causes and movements: "Activists publicized the environmental damage caused by the factory."
  • Research and findings: "Scientists publicized the results of their study to raise awareness."
  • Scandals and controversies: "The news channel publicized the CEO's internal emails."
  • Government and policy: "The health department publicized the new vaccination schedule."

Certain words pair with "publicize" so often that knowing them helps you sound natural:

  • Widely publicized — something that has been made known to a very large number of people. "The trial was widely publicized."
  • Heavily publicized — publicized with a lot of effort and intensity. "It was a heavily publicized product launch."
  • Poorly publicized — not publicized well enough; few people found out about it. "The workshop was poorly publicized, so only five people showed up."
  • Well-publicized — effectively and successfully made known. "Her visit to the city was a well-publicized event."
The full family of the word

The verb "publicize" belongs to a family of related words you will encounter:

  • Publicize — the verb itself (to publicize something)
  • Publicized — the past tense or adjective form (a publicized event)
  • Publicizing — the present participle (they are publicizing the campaign)
  • Publicity — the noun form; refers to the attention or coverage that something receives as a result of publicizing (The movie generated enormous publicity.)
  • Publicist — a person whose job is to publicize others (celebrities, authors, companies) (Her publicist arranged the interviews.)
One-sentence summary to lock it in
To publicize something is to deliberately and actively spread information about it to a wide audience, with the goal of making as many people as possible aware of it.
